t6.matrix-ops:
*When:* A problem asks for a product, sum, transpose or trace of matrices, or for the size of a result.

*Why:* Matrix multiplication pairs rows of the left factor with columns of the right factor. That pairing fixes both the size rule and the failure of commutativity.

*Move:*
$$(AB)_{ij}=\sum_k A_{ik}B_{kj},\qquad (AB)^T=B^TA^T$$
Check that the inner sizes match, since an $m\times n$ times an $n\times p$ matrix is $m\times p$. Dot row $i$ of $A$ with column $j$ of $B$. For a transpose of a product, reverse the order. The trace is the sum of the diagonal entries, and $\operatorname{tr}(cA)=c\operatorname{tr}A$.

*Example:* Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{pmatrix}4&1\\2&0\end{pmatrix}$. Each entry is a row-column dot product. The top-left entry is $1\cdot4+2\cdot2=8$. Swapping the order gives a different matrix.
$$AB=\begin{pmatrix}8&1\\6&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad BA=\begin{pmatrix}4&11\\2&4\end{pmatrix}$$

*Trap:* Assuming $AB=BA$, as the example shows is false, or writing $(AB)^T=A^TB^T$ with the order unchanged.

*Check:* The result has the row count of the left factor and the column count of the right factor.
t6.gauss:
*When:* A linear system must be solved, or a rank, pivot count or echelon form is asked for.

*Why:* Three row operations never change the solution set, and they turn a tangled system into a staircase that can be read off from the bottom up.

*Move:*
$$R_i\to R_i-c\,R_j$$
The allowed operations are swapping two rows, scaling a row by a nonzero number, and adding a multiple of one row to another. Work column by column. Pick a pivot, then clear every entry below it. For a system, reduce the augmented matrix and read the answers from the bottom row up. The rank is the number of nonzero rows left.

*Example:* Reduce the matrix below.
$$\begin{pmatrix}1&2&1\\2&5&3\\1&3&2\end{pmatrix}\xrightarrow{R_2-2R_1,\;R_3-R_1}\begin{pmatrix}1&2&1\\0&1&1\\0&1&1\end{pmatrix}\xrightarrow{R_3-R_2}\begin{pmatrix}1&2&1\\0&1&1\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}$$
There are two pivots, so the rank is $2$.

*Trap:* Scaling a row by $0$, which destroys an equation. A row reading $0=5$ means the system has no solution.

*Check:* The rank never exceeds the number of rows or columns.
t6.determinant:
*When:* A square matrix needs an invertibility test, a volume factor, or a product or power of determinants.

*Why:* The determinant is the signed volume scale of the map. It is zero exactly when the map flattens space, so the matrix is not invertible.

*Move:*
$$\det\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}=ad-bc,\qquad \det(AB)=\det A\,\det B,\qquad \det(cA)=c^n\det A$$
For $2\times2$ use the formula. For larger sizes, row-reduce to triangular form and multiply the diagonal. Each row swap flips the sign. Adding a multiple of one row to another changes nothing.

*Example:* Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&1\\3&5&2\\1&0&4\end{pmatrix}$. Subtract $3R_1$ from $R_2$ and $R_1$ from $R_3$, then subtract $2R_2$ from $R_3$. The diagonal becomes $1,-1,5$, so
$$\det A=-5,\qquad \det(3A)=3^3(-5)=-135$$

*Trap:* Writing $\det(cA)=c\det A$. Every one of the $n$ rows picks up the factor $c$.

*Check:* A zero determinant must match dependent rows or columns.
t6.inverse:
*When:* A system $A\mathbf x=\mathbf b$ must be solved by inverting, or $A^{-1}$ or a product of inverses is needed.

*Why:* The inverse undoes $A$. It exists only when $A$ does not collapse any direction, which means $\det A\neq0$.

*Move:*
$$\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}^{-1}=\frac{1}{ad-bc}\begin{pmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{pmatrix},\qquad (AB)^{-1}=B^{-1}A^{-1}$$
Compute $ad-bc$ first. If it is zero, stop, because no inverse exists. Otherwise swap the two diagonal entries, negate the other two, and divide everything by the determinant. For larger matrices, row-reduce the block matrix $[A\mid I]$ until the left half is $I$. The right half is then $A^{-1}$.

*Example:* Invert $A=\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\5&2\end{pmatrix}$. The determinant is $6-5=1$, so no division is needed. Swap $3$ and $2$, then negate $1$ and $5$.
$$A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-5&3\end{pmatrix}$$

*Trap:* Forgetting the minus signs on $b$ and $c$, or the factor $\frac1{\det}$.

*Check:* Multiply $AA^{-1}$ and look for $I$.
t6.vector-spaces:
*When:* A set of vectors, polynomials or matrices is claimed to be a subspace, or a solution set is described.

*Why:* A subspace is a set that stays inside itself under the two basic operations. Anything that can be built from its members by adding and scaling must also be a member.

*Move:*
$$\mathbf 0\in W,\qquad \mathbf u,\mathbf v\in W\Rightarrow \mathbf u+\mathbf v\in W,\qquad c\mathbf u\in W$$
Test the zero vector first, since a failure there ends the question. Then check closure for general $\mathbf u,\mathbf v$ and every scalar $c$. Sets cut out by $A\mathbf x=\mathbf 0$ always pass.

*Example:* Is $W=\{(x,y,z): x=2z\}$ a subspace of $\mathbb R^3$? The zero vector fits. Take two members and add them.
$$(2z_1,y_1,z_1)+(2z_2,y_2,z_2)=(2(z_1+z_2),\,y_1+y_2,\,z_1+z_2)\in W$$
Scaling works the same way, so $W$ is a subspace.

*Trap:* Testing one pair of numbers. Closure must hold for all members.

*Check:* A set with a constant term like $x+y=1$ misses $\mathbf 0$.
t6.basis-dim:
*When:* A question asks about span, independence, a basis, or the dimension of a space or subspace.

*Why:* A basis is the smallest set that still reaches everything. Its size is the same for every basis, so it measures the space.

*Move:*
$$c_1\mathbf v_1+\cdots+c_k\mathbf v_k=\mathbf 0\;\Rightarrow\;\text{all }c_i=0\quad(\text{independent})$$
Put the vectors as columns of a matrix and row-reduce. The pivot columns are independent, and their count is the dimension of the span. In $\mathbb R^n$, more than $n$ vectors are always dependent, and fewer than $n$ never span.

*Example:* Find the dimension of the span of $(1,0,1)$, $(0,1,1)$, $(1,1,2)$. The third is the sum of the first two, so it adds nothing.
$$\begin{pmatrix}1&0&1\\0&1&1\\1&1&2\end{pmatrix}\to\begin{pmatrix}1&0&1\\0&1&1\\0&1&1\end{pmatrix}\to\begin{pmatrix}1&0&1\\0&1&1\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}$$
Two pivots, so the dimension is $2$.

*Trap:* Counting the vectors given instead of the pivots.

*Check:* The dimension cannot exceed the number of vectors or the ambient size.
t6.rank-nullity:
*When:* A matrix or linear map has its rank, kernel, image or nullity asked for, and one of them is known.

*Why:* Each input direction either survives into the image or is crushed into the kernel. Together they use up the whole domain.

*Move:*
$$\operatorname{rank}T+\dim\ker T=\dim V$$
Here $V$ is the domain. For an $m\times n$ matrix the domain is $\mathbb R^n$, so $n$ is the column count. Find what is given, then subtract from $n$. The rank is also the number of pivots and the dimension of the column space.

*Example:* A matrix has $9$ columns and $6$ rows, and its rank is $6$. The nullity comes from the column count.
$$\dim\ker=9-6=3$$
The image sits inside $\mathbb R^6$ and has dimension $6$, so it fills the target.

*Trap:* Subtracting from the row count. The rows give the size of the target, not the domain.

*Check:* The rank is at most the smaller of the row and column counts.
t6.lin-maps:
*When:* A map $T$ is given by a rule and you must test linearity, build its matrix, or find its kernel or image.

*Why:* A linear map is fixed by what it does to the basis vectors. Knowing $T(e_1),\dots,T(e_n)$ gives the whole map.

*Move:*
$$T(\mathbf u+\mathbf v)=T\mathbf u+T\mathbf v,\qquad T(c\mathbf u)=cT\mathbf u,\qquad [T]=\big(T(e_1)\;\cdots\;T(e_n)\big)$$
Check the two rules, or spot a constant term that breaks them. Apply $T$ to each standard basis vector and write the results as columns. The kernel solves $T\mathbf x=\mathbf 0$.

*Example:* Let $T(x,y,z)=(x-z,\;2y+z)$. Apply it to $e_1$, $e_2$, $e_3$ in turn.
$$[T]=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&-1\\0&2&1\end{pmatrix}$$

*Trap:* Writing the results as rows instead of columns, or calling $T(x,y)=(x+3,y)$ linear when $T(\mathbf 0)\neq\mathbf 0$.

*Check:* The matrix has one column per input coordinate.
t6.change-basis:
*When:* A vector or map must be written in a new basis, or two matrices are claimed to represent the same map.

*Why:* The map does not change, only the coordinates do. The matrix $P$ translates between the two coordinate systems.

*Move:*
$$\mathbf x=P\,[\mathbf x]_{\mathcal B},\qquad B=P^{-1}AP$$
Let $P$ have the new basis vectors as columns. Then $P$ turns new coordinates into standard ones. To get new coordinates from standard ones, solve $P\mathbf c=\mathbf x$. Similar matrices share trace, determinant and eigenvalues.

*Example:* Basis $\mathbf b_1=(1,2)$ and $\mathbf b_2=(0,1)$. Find the coordinates of $\mathbf x=(3,7)$.
$$c_1(1,2)+c_2(0,1)=(3,7)\Rightarrow c_1=3,\;c_2=1$$
The coordinates are $(3,1)$.

*Trap:* Using $P^T$ or $PAP^{-1}$ in the wrong order. The inverse goes on the left of $A$.

*Check:* Multiply $P[\mathbf x]_{\mathcal B}$ and recover $\mathbf x$.
t6.eigen-2x2:
*When:* A $2\times2$ matrix needs eigenvalues, or its trace and determinant are linked to them.

*Why:* An eigenvector is only stretched by $A$. That happens exactly when $A-\lambda I$ is singular, so its determinant vanishes.

*Move:*
$$\lambda^2-(\operatorname{tr}A)\,\lambda+\det A=0$$
Here $\operatorname{tr}A$ is the sum of the diagonal entries. Compute the trace and determinant, write the quadratic, and solve it. The roots add to the trace and multiply to the determinant, so $\lambda_1^2+\lambda_2^2=(\operatorname{tr}A)^2-2\det A$.

*Example:* Take $A=\begin{pmatrix}5&1\\2&4\end{pmatrix}$, with trace $9$ and determinant $20-2=18$.
$$\lambda^2-9\lambda+18=(\lambda-3)(\lambda-6)=0$$
The eigenvalues are $3$ and $6$.

*Trap:* Using $+\operatorname{tr}A$ in the middle term, or a wrong sign on the determinant term.

*Check:* The two roots must sum to $9$ and multiply to $18$.
t6.diagonalize:
*When:* A power $A^k$ is wanted, or you must decide whether $A=PDP^{-1}$ exists.

*Why:* In an eigenbasis the matrix just scales each axis, so powers become powers of the scalars.

*Move:*
$$A=PDP^{-1}\;\Rightarrow\;A^k=PD^kP^{-1}$$
Here $D$ holds the eigenvalues and $P$ holds matching eigenvectors as columns. Find the eigenvalues, then each eigenspace by solving $(A-\lambda I)\mathbf v=\mathbf 0$. Also $\operatorname{tr}A^k=\sum\lambda_i^k$ and $\det A^k=\prod\lambda_i^k$. The matrix diagonalizes exactly when the eigenvectors fill a basis. Distinct eigenvalues always suffice.

*Example:* Eigenvalues $1$ and $-2$ for a $2\times2$ matrix $A$. Then $\operatorname{tr}(A^4)$ and $\det(A^4)$ follow without finding $P$.
$$\operatorname{tr}(A^4)=1^4+(-2)^4=17,\qquad \det(A^4)=(-2)^4=16$$

*Trap:* Assuming every matrix diagonalizes. A repeated eigenvalue with a one-dimensional eigenspace fails.

*Check:* The product of the diagonal entries of $D$ must equal $\det A$.
t6.cayley-ham:
*When:* A high power of a small matrix, or its inverse, is needed without diagonalizing.

*Why:* A matrix satisfies its own characteristic polynomial. That lets you rewrite any higher power in terms of lower ones.

*Move:*
$$A^2-(\operatorname{tr}A)A+(\det A)I=0$$
This is the $2\times2$ case. Solve it for $A^2$ in terms of $A$ and $I$. Multiply by $A$ again to reduce $A^3$, and repeat for higher powers. To get the inverse, move the $I$ term alone to one side, then factor $A$ out of the other side.

*Example:* Let $\operatorname{tr}A=4$ and $\det A=1$, so $A^2=4A-I$. Then the cube follows.
$$A^3=4A^2-A=4(4A-I)-A=15A-4I$$

*Trap:* Dropping the determinant term, or substituting the scalar $\det A$ where $\det A\,I$ belongs.

*Check:* Take traces of $A^3=15A-4I$: $15\cdot4-4\cdot2=52$, which equals $\lambda_1^3+\lambda_2^3=4^3-3\cdot1\cdot4$.
t6.inner-product:
*When:* Lengths, angles, orthogonality or projections appear, or an orthogonal basis must be built.

*Why:* The dot product measures how much two vectors point the same way. Removing that shared part leaves a perpendicular piece.

*Move:*
$$\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf u}\mathbf v=\frac{\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf u}{\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf u}\,\mathbf u$$
Here $\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=\sum u_iv_i$ and the length is $\|\mathbf v\|=\sqrt{\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf v}$. Vectors are orthogonal when their dot product is $0$. For Gram-Schmidt, keep $\mathbf u_1=\mathbf v_1$. Then subtract from each later vector its projections onto the earlier ones, and divide by the length at the end if unit vectors are wanted.

*Example:* Take $\mathbf v_1=(1,2)$ and $\mathbf v_2=(3,1)$. Subtract the projection of $\mathbf v_2$ onto $\mathbf v_1$.
$$\mathbf u_2=(3,1)-\frac{5}{5}(1,2)=(2,-1)$$
Check that $(1,2)\cdot(2,-1)=0$.

*Trap:* Dividing by $\|\mathbf u\|$ instead of $\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf u$ in the projection formula.

*Check:* The leftover vector must have dot product $0$ with the one removed.
t6.spectral:
*When:* A real symmetric matrix or a quadratic form $\mathbf x^TA\mathbf x$ is given, and its extreme values or definiteness matter.

*Why:* A symmetric matrix has perpendicular eigen-directions. In those directions the form is a plain sum of scaled squares.

*Move:*
$$A=QDQ^T,\qquad \mathbf x^TA\mathbf x=\sum_i\lambda_i y_i^2\;\text{ with }\;\mathbf y=Q^T\mathbf x$$
Find the eigenvalues, which are always real. On the unit sphere the form runs from the smallest to the largest eigenvalue. All $\lambda_i>0$ means positive definite.

*Example:* Find the maximum of $3x^2+4xy$ on $x^2+y^2=1$. The matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}3&2\\2&0\end{pmatrix}$ with trace $3$ and determinant $-4$.
$$\lambda^2-3\lambda-4=0\;\Rightarrow\;\lambda=4,\,-1$$
The maximum is $4$.

*Trap:* Taking the cross term $6xy$ itself as the off-diagonal entry. Each off-diagonal entry is half of it.

*Check:* The eigenvalues must add to the trace.
t6.jordan-nilpotent:
*When:* A matrix has $N^k=0$ for some $k$, or a Jordan block structure or minimal polynomial is needed.

*Why:* A nilpotent matrix shifts vectors down a chain until they vanish. The chain length decides the smallest power that gives zero.

*Move:*
$$N^k=0\;\Rightarrow\;\text{only eigenvalue }0,\qquad N^m\neq0\text{ for }m<k$$
The minimal polynomial is $x^k$ for the smallest such $k$. A single Jordan block of size $s$ with eigenvalue $0$ has $N^{s-1}\neq0$ and $N^s=0$. The number of blocks is $\dim\ker N$, and the block sizes add up to $n$. So $\operatorname{rank}N=n-(\text{number of blocks})$.

*Example:* A $4\times4$ Jordan block has ones on the superdiagonal. Its first, second and third powers are nonzero, and
$$N^3\neq0,\qquad N^4=0,\qquad \dim\ker N=1$$
So the minimal polynomial is $x^4$.

*Trap:* Concluding $N=0$ from $N^2=0$. A nonzero matrix can still square to zero.

*Check:* The index $k$ can never exceed the matrix size.
